title: Betsy and the Moonlight Path
markdown:
Betsy the beaver loved her home by Whispering Creek. It was a happy, familiar place, always filled with the comforting smell of damp earth and the gentle, musical gurgle of the water flowing by. Betsy spent her days as busy as a bee, patting mud into place and carefully adding sturdy twigs to her ever-growing dam. Her lodge was the coziest place in the entire woods, wonderfully warm and perfectly dry, and it always smelled faintly of fresh pine needles. Betsy felt completely safe here, nestled amongst the reeds and the rustling trees. She knew every tiny ripple, every secret rustle in the tall grass, every single shadow that danced on the water. It was her happy, familiar world, and she wouldn't have it any other way.

One evening, as the sun began to dip below the horizon, painting the sky in shades of orange and purple, Betsy decided her lodge needed something extra special. "Moon-moss!" she chirped excitedly to herself, her whiskers twitching with a grand idea. "That's exactly what will make my lodge extra, extra cozy for the moonbeams!" She knew that the most beautiful moon-moss, the kind that practically glowed, only grew on the far side of Whispering Creek. This was a place where the shadows grew long and very, very deep. Betsy knew she would have to cross the water to get it, but as she thought about it, a little shiver ran right down her furry spine. The creek looked so dark and seemed so very, very wide when the sun said goodnight. Betsy’s paws felt a little clammy, and her tail gave a nervous little flick. This is fear, she realized with a small sigh, fear of the deep, dark water.

Betsy took a deep breath and puffed out her chest. "I can build a bridge," she declared bravely, though her voice wobbled just a tiny bit. "A special night bridge!" Her plan was to gather the sturdiest, strongest branches she could find and weave them all together. The moon, a slender sliver of silver light, was just beginning to peek out from behind the gathering dark clouds. Betsy knew she would have to venture into the parts of the creek she usually avoided when the sun tucked itself away. The very thought of the dark, unknown water made her tummy do a funny little flip-flop. If she didn't gather the moon-moss soon, the rare fireflies that only visited during the fullest moon would also leave, and Betsy loved watching their twinkling dance!

With a determined wiggle of her nose, Betsy waded into the cool water at the edge of the creek. The soft, squishy mud felt funny between her toes. She tried to carry a long, heavy branch towards the middle of the creek, but it was just too slippery and fell with a loud splash! Betsy flinched, her ears perking up. The sound seemed so incredibly loud in the hushed quiet of the night. She could only see vague shapes in the dim moonlight, and every shadow seemed to twist and stretch, looking like a wobbly, wiggly monster. She tried to push a big, fallen log into place to help make her bridge, but it just bobbed and floated away, as if playing a game of tag with the current. Suddenly, a very loud ribbit echoed from the tall reeds nearby. Betsy froze completely still. Her heart thumped like a tiny, frantic drum against her ribs. This is too scary, she thought, her whiskers drooping with worry. I should just go back. She almost turned around, ready to give up, her brave beaver spirit feeling very small indeed.

Just then, a soft, almost musical croak drifted from a large, velvety lily pad floating nearby. Croak! As the sound left the lily pad, a shimmering silver stone, glowing with a gentle light, popped into existence right on the water's surface! Betsy blinked her eyes, utterly amazed. Another gentle croak, and another silver stone appeared, and then another, forming a wobbly little path. Peeking out from behind a large, leafy fern was a small, round frog with the most amazing eyes she had ever seen; they seemed to hold tiny, captured pieces of the moon itself. "Hello," whispered the frog, her voice as delicate as tiny bells tinkling in the breeze. "I'm Oona. I can make stepping-stones, if you like. They're made of moonlight and wishes." Betsy’s eyes widened with wonder. She had found the perfect answer to her bridge problem, and something even more wonderful than she could have imagined – a friend who could make actual magic!

Betsy tentatively hopped onto the first silver stone. It felt surprisingly cool and wonderfully smooth beneath her paws. Oona gave another happy croak, and more stones appeared, stretching all the way across the creek, like a glittering pathway leading to the other side. Betsy reached the far bank and quickly gathered the soft, gently glowing moon-moss, its light making her paws feel warm. As she turned to come back, she saw Oona sitting all alone on her lily pad. Oona looked a little sad, her shining eyes gazing out at the water. Betsy suddenly realised that while making stepping-stones was a wonderful trick, it was also a little bit lonely without anyone to share it with. Betsy really wanted to share her cozy lodge, but if she took Oona with her, she wouldn't have her special stones to get back across the water. She would have to leave her half-built bridge behind, unfinished and perhaps forgotten. Betsy hesitated, her paws still on the soft moss. She pictured her lodge, warm and dry, with the moonlight dappling through the reeds. But then, her gaze fell upon Oona’s wide, lonely eyes, which seemed to hold all the quiet sadness of the night. A flutter of warmth, like a tiny spark, ignited deep in Betsy’s chest, a feeling that shone brighter than any moonbeam. It was the feeling of knowing what was truly important. With a soft sigh, she let go of the thought of her unfinished bridge, the sturdy branches now just twigs at the mercy of the creek, and turned fully towards her new friend. The loss of her own work was a small price for this new, glowing warmth.

"Oona," Betsy said, her voice warm and inviting, "would you like to come to my lodge? I have plenty of room, and it's very cozy inside. We can even share some berry tea!" Oona's big eyes lit up like tiny lanterns. Ribbit! she chirped happily, a sound full of delight. Betsy stepped back onto the silver stones, and Oona croaked a shimmering path for them both. The stones gleamed, leading them over the dark, deep water, not just to Betsy's side, but all the way back towards the warmth and safety of the lodge. Betsy didn't need to finish her bridge tonight. She had Oona, and that was much, much better.

Betsy and Oona sat together by the crackling fire in Betsy's lodge, sipping sweet berry tea from little acorn cups. The soft, glowing moon-moss Betsy had gathered made the whole place shimmer with a gentle light. Betsy no longer felt even a tiny shiver when she thought about the creek. Even when the wind rustled the reeds by the water's edge, making them whisper secrets, Betsy knew she could always ask Oona to make a path of shimmering light if she ever wanted to visit the other side again. The sound of Oona’s happy giggles, mixing with the gentle gurgle of Whispering Creek, was the best bridge of all.
characters: Betsy the beaver, Oona the moon-frog
